status: Source-fit authoring design after original-clause/whole-claim/resource review; frozen for final combined independent review, not learner attainment.

resources.role: Actually inspected original1811map supplies broad Upper/Lower Canada and waterway geography. All later case annotations remain explicitly dated teaching additions; no prejudicial labels or blank-land inference.

facts: The reviewed Fort William account identifies the Anishinaabe Lake Superior setting and traditional use as distinct from the later1853reserve.
The actual Six Nations Haldimand account identifies1784land along the Grand River and the Crown-alliance/relocation context.
limits: Upper/Lower Canada are historical colonial regional references, not a claim that they exhaust traditional Indigenous territories.
A modern reserve outline is not the full earlier territory or proof of every treaty term.

facts: The actual account locates Kahnawà:ke near Montréal and describes Kanien’keha:ka political/kinship and fur-trade relationships, including the1813defence of the Montréal approach.
The broad Montréal location places this studied First Nation community in the Lower Canada part of the dated map, while its traditional relationships extend beyond a colonial provincial label.
limits: Use only checked location and relationship facts. The page’s unnecessary1814BeaverDam battle date is not adopted or repaired.
Do not identify all Haudenosaunee communities as Kahnawà:ke or turn a colonial label into current legal title.

facts: The already reviewed timeline describes the1828Drummond Island to Penetanguishene movement in the Georgian Bay setting. Use the attributed cause/date and label the source account.
limits: The1828movement is not something the1811map itself depicts.
A historical community-location task does not adjudicate modern citizenship, consultation territories or contested land rights.
Do not adopt unrelated timeline date typos or label every mixed-ancestry fur trader Métis.

facts: Previously reviewed Traill1832–35Peterborough/Katchewanooka-area and Buxton1849–1850settler cases supply two different located settler communities.

Traill LetterVIII November1832and LetterXII November1833describe tree cutting/burning and replacing wooded land with farm fields/crops; use the factual landscape change without adopting her celebratory judgments or speculative climate explanation.
limits: The locations are separately dated case markers on a reference base, not claims that Buxton1849or the later Peterborough settlement was already depicted in1811.
No live burning/clearing task or invented regional percentage is required.

resources.publisher: Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation
facts: The actual Toronto account relates Crown communication/supply and linked settlement objectives, York’s capital location, disputed land boundaries and the1805agreement.
The actual Ajetance account describes settler inflow into lands/fisheries weakening the Mississaugas’ economy before the1818agreement.
limits: The resource supplies actual effects/pressure, not a claim every settler settlement had identical outcomes or every treaty fairly resolved the issues.
Do not add an unmeasured urban land-cover loss or fish-population number. Modern cities mentioned by the page are not automatically1818cities.

actions: Use the actual dated base and source accounts to identify and broadly locate Anishinaabe Fort William/Lake Superior, Six Nations/Grand River and Kahnawà:ke/Montréal, plus the studied Métis Drummond Island/Penetanguishene movement. Identify Upper and Lower Canada on the map while retaining the communities’ own names and source accounts.

Distinguish traditional territory/use from relocation and a later reserve or colonial border. Record the actual1784Six Nations and1828Métis movement context; describe why a source says a community moved or was displaced, rather than assuming every movement was free choice or every current reserve is an ancestral boundary.

Create a labelled source-attributed map with a key distinguishing a studied place, broad earlier-use area and dated movement. A broad arrow communicates the described movement, not a reconstructed exact travel track. Locate the Lower Canada case as well as the Upper Canada cases; do not treat Ontario today as the whole historical task.
communities-in-historical-regions.positive: Identifies various First Nations and studied Métis communities across the historical Upper/Lower Canada reference, includes both traditional use and relocation and supports locations with the actual sources.
limits: The source examples do not require an exhaustive community inventory or every named Métis community in each colonial region.
Location knowledge does not certify legal boundaries, present-day identity eligibility or all period-life facts.
communities-in-historical-regions.transfer: Given a changed map orientation and one new attributed place/date card, place the broad case correctly and explain whether the card establishes traditional use, movement or neither.

actions: Identify the two reviewed settler cases: Traill’s1832–35Upper Canada household/neighbour setting and Black settlers at Buxton1849–1850. Explain that these are different communities and not the whole settler population.

Locate each broadly using actual source place references and the labelled map/key; retain the period beside the marker. Explain their relation to a named lake/river or reference town without inventing an1811label for a later settlement.
Transfer to a changed regional map with the same accurately attributed source card. Do not infer a population’s ethnicity or settlement date merely from a modern place name.
settler-communities-and-location.positive: Identifies and locates more than one source-supported settler community in the selected period, using the actual dated case evidence.
limits: No obligation is inferred to cover every illustrative national/ethnic group.
The record permits an appropriate map medium; the separate A2.3both-media obligation remains in its own protocol.

actions: Compare different settlement kinds using actual evidence: rural farm clearing in Traill’s1832–33account and Crown-linked homestead/capital-town development in the Mississaugas’ Toronto/Ajetance histories. Identify the purpose and type of settlement before explaining effects.

For the natural environment, use the documented conversion of trees/wooded ground to cleared farm fields and the actual pressure on the Mississaugas’ lands/fisheries. For existing communities, explain the source-described consequences for the Mississaugas’ economy, land use and contested agreements. These are distinct source-grounded effects, not a universal ecological ranking of peoples.

Explain both natural-environment and existing-community impacts across the compared cases. Separate the land transformation a source directly describes from an unmeasured proposed further consequence. A source’s celebratory account of clearing does not establish that everyone benefited.

Transfer to a new short documented settlement account: identify an evidenced environmental effect and any evidenced effect on an existing community, or state what is unknown rather than filling the gap.
settlement-effects.positive: Describes source-supported impacts of different settlement kinds on the natural setting and existing communities, preserving actual period/party and evidence limits.
limits: No invented hectares, wildlife trend, urban pollution or precise historical land-cover map.
Different map dates or current boundaries do not prove that the exact same land was affected in an undocumented way.

boundaries: Seven proposed component extensions use exact existing CA8–9contexts; no new topic, claim expansion, age interval, edge or teaching guide.
Additional case references instantiate the existing bounded period knowledge and shared map operation; no node is created per community or current country outline.
A3overall remains separately pending its integrated relationships/land account; A1later-policy and identity obligations remain separate.
Authoring source fit is not observed pupil performance or a present-day land-rights determination.
